background.definition: Tularemia is a disease with multiple presentations caused by the zoonotic bacteria Francisella tularensis.

list.listitem: Less than 200 cases per year in the United States. However, it is likely underrecognized and underreported.
American Indians/Alaska Natives: 0.5/100,000.
Caucasians: 0.04/100,000.
African American and Asians/Pacific Islanders: 0.01/100,000.
Most cases are sporadic or in small clusters. Tularemia has been reported in all states except Hawaii.

In Turkey, among 317 patients admitted with clinical suspicion for tularemia, 49 were confirmed to have the disease. It was more likely in older persons living in rural areas, and those with reported contact with rodents.
Tularensis is one of the most pathogenic bacteria know. As few as 10 organisms can initiate disease in humans.
Tularemia has had a recent surge in interest as a potential to be used as a biological weapon; it is a reportable disease in the United States.

Tularemia is caused by a zoonotic small, nonmotile, aerobic, Gram-negative coccobacillus Francisella tularensis. There are currently 4 subspecies, with only 2 accounting for most of the human disease. These subspecies are serologically indistinguishable.
Subspecies tularensis (Type A) is more virulent and is most common in the United States.
Subspecies holarctica (Type B) causes less severe disease and is most common in Europe and Asia.
The natural reservoirs for these bacteria are voles, mice, water rats, squirrels, rabbits, and hares.
Human infection is acquired by arthropod bite, handling infected animal tissue or fluid, contact or ingestion of contaminated food, water, or soil, and inhalation of infective aerosols.
Arthropods that can spread tularemia include but are not limited to ticks, flies, and mosquitoes.
Tularensis is a facultative intracellular bacterium that replicates in macrophages. It targets lymph nodes, lungs, spleen, liver, and kidneys.
Wear DEET-type insect repellents when hiking and camping, avoid handling sick or dead wild animals, and do not eat raw or undercooked wild animal meat products. C
Treat pets for fleas and ticks per veterinarian recommendations. C

Post-exposure prophylaxis is effective with both doxycycline and ciprofloxacin for 14 days (use oral dosages in ). It is only indicated in a person possibly exposed to F. tularensis, not in people with close contact to patients with tularemia. B
There is a potentially effective unlicensed live attenuated vaccine, but it is not currently recommended for use. C

Patients with abrupt onset of fever, profound lymphadenopathy, with or without typical skin lesion, and with evidence of arthropod bite, exposure to wild animals, or contaminated water should be tested for tularemia. C
Standard blood and wound cultures are often negative. C
Positive culture, fourfold increase in serum antibody titer, a single agglutination titer of 1:160 or greater, or a single microagglutination titer 1:128 or greater are diagnostic. C

Develops more rapidly, mediastinal widening due to edema or bleeding, bacterial toxin
Usually milder in symptoms, longer incubation period
More prevalent during the winter, distinguish using rapid antigen detection assay

Differential.Differential_Features: Greater local inflammation and pain, less systemic symptoms
Antibody and antigen assays will differentiate, slower progression

list.listitem: Diagnostic criteria defined by CDC are shown below.
Presumptive/probable case: elevated serum antibody titer less than 1:160 or detection of F. tularensis in a clinical specimen by fluorescent assay.

Confirmed case: isolation of F. tularensis in a clinical specimen, Four fold or greater increase in serum antibody titer, or 1:160 or greater serum agglutination antibody titer, or 1:128 or greater microagglutination titer in a patient with typical symptoms.
Tularemia is characterized by multiple clinical forms. See for descriptions of each clinical manifestation of tularemia.

Patients typically present with abrupt onset fever to 38°C to 40°C, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, coryza, and sore throat. See and . It should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients with prolonged fever and risk factors for exposure.
The incubation period is 3 to 5 days (CDC).

In a series of 68 cases in Turkey, the most common symptoms were sore throat (100%), fever (96% in children, 91% in adults), tonsillitis (69% and 79%), and rash (15% and 12%) with a mean duration of symptoms of 21 days in children and 33 days in adults. A series of 16 cases in a Turkish Military Hospital had generally similar findings.
The diagnosis is supported by evidence of arthropod bite, exposure to tissues of a mammalian host, or exposure to contaminated water.
As many as 42% to 50% of patients will have pulse-temperature dissociation (relative bradycardia in a febrile patient).
The WBC is typically normal to mildly elevated and can show a relative increase in mononuclear cells.
Liver enzymes may be mildly elevated.
C-reactive protein peaks at about 50 mg/L and sedimentation rate is usually elevated at 30 to 50 mm/hour.

Tularensis can be difficult to grow with standard blood and wound cultures. It is slow growing and requires a cysteine supplemented media. Blood cultures are rarely positive. Appropriate specimens include swabs or scrapings of ulcers, lymph node aspirates or biopsies, pharyngeal swabs, or respiratory specimens (e.g. pleural fluid), depending on the form of illness.

Serum antibody titer or agglutination and adapted microagglutination tests approach 100% sensitivity and specificity and are the most widely used tests to diagnose tularemia. However, these test can have cross-reactivity to Brucella, Yersinia enterocolitica, and Proteus. They appear in the second week following exposure, peak in several weeks, and then slowly decline. Patients can have a positive titer for several years.

An ELISA test can be used but has limited advantage over the more frequently used agglutination test. IgA, IgM, and IgG all raise and fall in parallel, and therefore are not useful in determining acute versus past infection. Sensitivity and specificity are 98%.
The CDC recommends direct immunofluorescence assay or PCR to support the diagnosis.
After an incubation period of 3 to 5 days, patients present with 1 of 7 clinical forms ().
With all clinical forms, onset is usually abrupt and is accompanied by fever to 38°C to 40°C, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, coryza, and sore throat.
Initial testing should include a serum antibody titer or agglutination tests.
First-line treatment is with streptomycin or gentamicin ().
First-line treatment includes gentamicin, ciprofloxacin and doxycycline (). Gentamicin is preferred for severe tularemia according to CDC guidance. A
Isolation is not needed as human-to-human transmission has not been reported. B
Tularemia is a reportable disease and clinicians should contact public health authorities of a suspected case. C

First-line treatment of tularemia is IV or IM gentamicin, IV or PO ciprofloxacin, or IV or PO doxycycline for 10 to 14 days. See . Gentamicin is preferred for severe tularemia according to CDC guidance.
Second-line treatment includes fluoroquinolones, doxycycline, and chloramphenicol for 14 to 21 days. See . B
Case reports (n=870) found mortality rates of 0.7% with gentamicin, 0.9% with fluoroquinolones, and 1.2% with tetracyclines.
Surgical drainage of lymph nodes may be necessary.
Human-to-human transmission is not known to occur. Isolation of hospitalized patients is not needed.
Inform microbiology laboratory personnel of a potential case of tularemia. A higher level of precaution is needed for laboratory works due to a risk of aerosolization of infective specimens.
Clinicians caring for patients with suspected tularemia should contact local or state health departments or if unavailable the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention at (970) 221-6400.
Referral to the hospital epidemiologist or infectious disease doctor is indicated.
Before antibiotics, the mortality rate for type A tularemia was 5% to 15% and as high as 30% to 60% in the respiratory form. Current mortality rate is less than 2%. B
The Type A biovar is more virulent and is more common in the United States. The Type B biovar rarely causes severe disease. B

The pneumonic form causes the highest morbidity and mortality. The most common form, ulceroglandular, rarely causes severe disease. Symptoms can be slow to resolve and lymphadenopathy can last for years. B
It is a rare cause of myocarditis.
Pregnancy loss has been reported and may be reduced by antimicrobial therapy, although this is based only on a small series of case reports.

feature.caption: Clinical Manifestations of Tularemia.
feature.feature_body:
Clinical Manifestations Description Cases (%)
Tularemia pneumonia Follows inhalation exposure 10-20
Acute flulike symptoms, progresses to severe pneumonia, bloody sputum, and can lead to respiratory failure and death
Chest radiograph shows peribronchial infiltrates, bronchopneumonia, pleural effusions, and hilar lymphadenopathy
Most likely form seen during an intentional release of tularemia
Ulceroglandular tularemia Follows handling contaminated material or arthropod bite 60-85
Papular lesion at the site of inoculation that enlarges to a pustule, ruptures to a painful ulcer that can be covered by an eschar. The ulcer is usually 0.4-3 cm
Accompanied by fever, body aches, and lymphadenopathy that can become fluctuant and rupture
Glandular tularemia Lymphadenopathy and fever without a skin lesion 3-15
Oculoglandular tularemia Follows direct contamination to the eyes 1-2
Purulent conjunctivitis, chemosis, conjunctival nodules or ulcers, or periorbital edema
Preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy
Oropharyngeal tularemia Follows ingestion of contaminated water or food 1-25
Exudative pharyngitis/tonsillitis, stomatitis, painful mucosal ulcerations, retropharyngeal abscess, regional lymphadenopathy
Tularemia sepsis Can be a complication of any form of tularemia infection
Septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, hemorrhage, acute respiratory distress syndrome, organ failure, and coma
Typhoidal tularemia Acute flulike symptoms with no indication of an inoculation site

feature.caption: Treatment of Tularemia (Source: https://www.cdc.gov/tularemia/clinicians/index.html)
feature.feature_body:
Drug Dosage Duration Comment
Adults
Gentamicin* 5 mg/kg IV or IM in 1 or 2 doses daily 10 - 14 days Fetal nerve deafness and renal damage have been reported with use of other aminoglycosides, but not gentamicin. Short-term use for treatment of tularemia likely poses little risk and the benefits likely outweigh the risks. Monitor serum drug levels.
Ciprofloxacin* 400 mg IV or 500 mg PO twice daily 10 - 14 days
Doxycycline 100 mg IV or PO twice daily 14 - 21 days
Children
Gentamicin* 2.5 mg/kg IM or IV 3 times daily** 10 - 14 days Monitor drug levels.
Ciprofloxacin* 15 mg/kg IV or PO twice daily ; maximum dose 800 mg per day 10 - 14 days
Doxycycline 2.2 mg/kg IV or PO twice daily; maximum dose 100 mg twice daily 21 days
*This is not a US Food and Drug Administration-approved use of this drug. NOTE: Combine aminoglycoside and fluoroquinolone in severe cases. Convert to oral medication when clinically indicated.
